paragraphs.text: Title: Machine Learning for Zero-Shot Generalization of Robotic Manipulation Policies Using Vision-Language Models
Summary:

Teaching robots to manipulate physical objects in unstructured environments remains one of the central challenges of embodied artificial intelligence. Traditional robot learning approaches require large amounts of task-specific demonstration data collected in the target environment, making them expensive to scale to new tasks or new scenes. Recent advances in large vision-language models have opened the possibility of using the rich semantic knowledge encoded in these models to guide robot policies toward novel objects and task instructions they have never encountered during training. This project investigates how pre-trained vision-language models can be adapted to serve as zero-shot policy modules for tabletop robotic manipulation, enabling a robot arm to follow natural language instructions and interact with previously unseen objects using simulated environments and publicly available demonstration datasets. No prior knowledge of robotics or machine learning is assumed. Detailed instructions and datasets will be provided to the student who takes the project.
Novelty:

Existing approaches to vision-language-conditioned robot manipulation either require fine-tuning large models on thousands of robot demonstrations, which is expensive, or use the language model only for high-level task decomposition while delegating low-level control to separately trained primitive skills. This project proposes a lightweight adapter architecture that grafts a small set of trainable cross-attention layers between a frozen vision-language model backbone and a diffusion-based action decoder, requiring fine-tuning of only the adapter parameters on a modest number of demonstrations while keeping the large pre-trained model frozen. The key novelty is a counterfactual data augmentation scheme in which the language instruction is systematically varied at training time while the visual scene is held fixed, or vice versa, forcing the adapter to disentangle visual and linguistic factors of variation and producing policies that are dramatically more robust to instruction paraphrasing and object appearance change at test time. This combination of parameter-efficient adaptation and counterfactual instruction augmentation is not present in the current robot learning literature and addresses a critical bottleneck for real-world deployment of generalist robot policies.
Datasets (all public, show dataset names and web addresses in text):

The Open X-Embodiment dataset aggregates over one million robot demonstrations across 22 robot embodiments and dozens of tasks collected by research groups worldwide and is available at https://robotics-transformer-x.github.io. The LIBERO benchmark provides 130 manipulation task suites in simulation with language annotations and is hosted at https://libero-project.github.io. The Bridge Dataset contains over 7,000 teleoperated demonstrations of kitchen manipulation tasks with language labels and can be downloaded at https://rail.eecs.berkeley.edu/datasets/bridge_release. The CLIPort benchmark for language-conditioned pick-and-place tasks in simulation is available at https://cliport.github.io. Together these four sources span simulation and real-robot demonstrations, diverse object sets, and language-annotated tasks at a scale sufficient for both adapter training and zero-shot generalization evaluation.

Research questions:

The primary research question is whether a lightweight cross-attention adapter trained on a small subset of the Open X-Embodiment demonstrations can match or exceed the zero-shot task success rate of fully fine-tuned baselines on novel objects and instructions from the LIBERO and CLIPort benchmarks. A secondary question is whether the counterfactual instruction augmentation strategy provides measurable improvement in robustness to instruction paraphrasing compared to standard data augmentation, as evaluated by testing the same physical task under a set of semantically equivalent but lexically diverse instruction phrasings. A third question is whether the adapter generalizes across robot embodiments, specifically whether an adapter trained on demonstrations from one robot arm in the Open X-Embodiment data retains reasonable performance when controlling a different simulated robot arm at test time.
Approach and Methods in detail:

The project is organized into four phases. In the first phase of approximately three months, the student will set up the simulation environment using the ManiSkill2 or PyBullet simulator and download the four datasets. A unified data loader will be written to parse demonstrations from all four sources into a common format consisting of a language instruction string, a sequence of RGB observation images at 224 by 224 pixels, and a sequence of end-effector pose actions represented as eight-dimensional vectors of position, quaternion, and gripper width. Demonstrations will be filtered to retain only those with valid language annotations and at least ten timesteps of action data.

In the second phase of approximately five months, the student will implement the adapter architecture. The frozen backbone will be the CLIP ViT-L/14 vision-language model, whose visual and textual encoders produce 1024-dimensional embeddings. The adapter consists of eight cross-attention layers with 512-dimensional keys and values, inserted after the frozen CLIP encoders, that take the visual token sequence and the language embedding as queries and keys respectively and produce a fused context vector. This context vector is passed to a conditional diffusion action decoder based on the DDPM formulation with a U-Net denoising network that takes as input a noisy action trajectory and the fused context and predicts the denoised trajectory. Only the adapter and the diffusion decoder are trained; CLIP weights remain frozen throughout.

In the third phase of approximately four months, the student will implement the counterfactual augmentation strategy. For each training demonstration, an augmented counterpart will be generated by replacing the original instruction with a semantically different instruction drawn from the same task suite but corresponding to a different goal, and the action sequence will be replaced with a null sequence of zeros, teaching the model that mismatched instruction-scene pairs should predict inaction. Additionally, paraphrase augmentations will be generated by prompting a locally hosted language model to produce five lexically diverse restatements of each original instruction, which are used as additional positive training examples. The student will compare four training conditions: no augmentation, paraphrase-only augmentation, counterfactual-only augmentation, and the full combined augmentation. Evaluation will be performed in simulation by rolling out the policy for 100 episodes per task split and measuring task success rate as the primary metric.

In the fourth phase of approximately two months, ablation studies will remove the adapter layers one at a time to assess the minimum number required for good performance, and a cross-embodiment transfer experiment will train on demonstrations from one robot type in Open X-Embodiment and evaluate on a different robot type in simulation. Qualitative analysis will examine cases where the policy fails due to visual ambiguity versus linguistic ambiguity by systematically holding one modality constant and varying the other.
Deliverables:

The student will produce a documented Python codebase using PyTorch hosted on GitHub, including simulation environment setup scripts, the data loading pipeline, the adapter and diffusion decoder implementation, training scripts, and evaluation rollout scripts. A written thesis of approximately 10,000 words covering background, methodology, experimental results, and discussion will be completed. A conference-length manuscript of approximately eight pages formatted to the CoRL or NeurIPS template will be prepared for peer-reviewed submission.

Regular Meeting?

I don’t require you to meet me regularly; however, I do require that you write me an email every 2 weeks to tell me what you did (attach any figures/tables) since your last email to me, so that I know your progress. The email can be quite brief or detailed. You are also welcome to set up a meeting with me. Kindly note that I may not respond to any of your emails; however, please be assured that I have read them and will respond if necessary. Occasionally, I may forget to reply even if I should reply, in which case, kindly remind me. Don’t apologize for lack of progress for various reasons, for example, being too busy with other courses, upcoming quiz, etc. No need to email me your codes or input data – I will need these only when you submit your final report. Email me any results, e.g., tables and figures. No need to list all papers you read or summarize papers you read.
A bad mistake is for the student not updating me regularly, wasting time on something not good, and suddenly telling me the deadline is due and too late to make any corrections/adjustments.

Your plan should be like this: you spend at most 2 months since my first email for reading existing work etc. Programming and running with data should start after that. The major part of your time will be spent on running program, test with data, modifying algorithms, compare results, etc. Don’t spend much time on planning, thinking, and writing report.
Get Started

You may need to study the tools to be used in your Project. For example, if you use neural networks, you can find a book in NTU library to read about the basics (you don’t need, but are welcome, to learn ALL about the tools or advanced materials). You could experiment it in Python (most popular programming language nowadays, although other language may still be used), with some tutorials, toolboxes and manuals. You can choose your preferred software environment / programming language for this Project. You can consider a neural network a black box, with inputs and outputs, plus some adjustable parameters. Once you have the neural network program and data, you can start training and testing, even without knowing much of the inner details of neural networks. So don’t overwhelm yourself with all that math and algorithms.

Most likely, you can find an existing program to use from public domain, without having to program from scratch. For example, https://paperswithcode.com/ has lots of papers with codes and data. But ultimately, you are responsible for coding. If you cannot find the code you like, you need to code yourself. Please don’t ask me to find things for you.

You also need to read some research papers published on your Project area. You need to understand what has been done and how it has been done, so that you know what to do in your project. Later you need to write about prior work in your report. In addition, while reading research papers, pay attention to how the papers are written, so that you know how to carry out your work and write your report properly. Your report should contain materials suitable for submission for publication in a journal (preferred) or conference.

To find research papers in the area of your Project, Google search may turn up low-quality (junk) papers and reading/learning junk leads to poor project outcome. Instead, go to the NTU Library website, click databases. Then find one of the reputable publisher, i.e., IEEE Xplore, Elsevier SicenceDirect, ACM, ACM, and SpringerLink, and search for only journal papers (not conference papers or book chapters).  Enter the keywords/phrases in your Project title/summary (use Advanced Search / enter multiple keywords to make your search more specific, only in paper title and abstract). Focus on more recent papers, e.g., recent 3-5 years. If you like, you could also search for Top-tier conferences, i.e., AAAI, ICML, CVPR, NeurIPS, ICCV, ECCV, ACM-MM (but not any other conferences). But in rare cases, if there are not many papers in the above places, you may have to google.
As I mentioned previously, this reading part should not last more than 2 months.
Goal of your Project
If there are already papers published on your topic, you should attempt to improve on the best published method on the subject.

First, reproduce the best published results in a research paper using a program (written yourself or already available for download) and the same data used in the paper. It is highly desirable to select the state-of-the-art to compare. Deliberately selecting an inferior or older approach to compare will be bad for your project. You should make sure the data used in the paper can be freely downloaded.
Second, make some modifications to the algorithms in the paper and try to improve the results for the same data used in the paper.
It would be less desirable to simply do something, without comparing with published research paper(s), or simply reproduce someone else’s results without trying any improvements.
If no prior work exists on your topic (rarely happens), you should try to propose your own solution to the problem, maybe inspired by some other solutions.

During your computer simulations, whenever appropriate, calculate averages and standard deviations. For example, if each time your run the simulation with different initialization, the result is different, you will need to run 5-10 times and computer the average/standard deviation.
Standardize the result presentations. For example, an accuracy of 53.5973% usually does not make sense and 53.6% would be sufficient.
Use tables and figures to present and compare results, rather than bullets. For comparison, each table should have multiple columns/rows and each figure should have more than 1 curve/dots.
Basically, learn from a good journal paper on how to carry out simulations, how to present your results, etc.
If the proposed method consists of multiple components, ablation studies should be performed to see which components are necessary.

Statistical significance between performance differences of different methods should be analyzed using statistical ranking methods, such as Wilcoxon test / Friedman test. Comparisons of different methods should be clearly presented in tables and/or figures. Each method should be denoted by an acronym and the year published, e.g., ResNet, 2022.

The purpose of this project is for you to learn something. There is no penalty if you tried a few ways but are not able to improve the results. You should include your attempts in your report. Do not fake any results, which will result in severe penalties. All results are subject to verification at the end of the project.
Data Preparation

Data should be divided into 3 sets: training set, validation set, and test set. The training set is used to train weights/biases. Validation set is used to determine the best hyperparameters, such as the number layers, the number of neurons in each layer, the learning rate, etc. If you use past data to predict future data, the number of past data (window length) used to predict the next data is also a hyperparameter to be determined. You need to search for the optimal set of hyperparameters. After that, test results are obtained using the optimal hyperparameters and the test data set.
Writing Reports/Dissertation
Do a spelling and grammar check.

Do not copy anyone else’s stuff, including sentences, paragraphs, figures, pictures, pseudo-codes, etc (it is against copyright law to do any of these). Write your own sentences. Draw your own figures (if you use software other than Microsoft Word to draw your figures, please also submit the figures in editable forms. For example, if you draw in ppt, also submit your ppt file). Do not include any scanned or copy-righted materials (even if you cite the source). Violations will result in penalties. Don’t ask for or try to achieve an “acceptable similarity score” in a Turnitin report. Instead, use the colored parts in the Turnitin report to make sure there are no copied sentences (except references, names, addresses). It is possible that something with 45% similarity score is alright (without copied materials), but something with 10% similarity score is not acceptable (with copied materials).

For each method/algorithm used: if it is invented by you, say "we propose...". If it is NOT invented by you, write "... was proposed by ... (give references. Use past tense). If it is your modification of someone else's work, say exactly what the modifications are and give references. You must review all existing work directly related to yours. Do not include other people's work that is not directly related to your results. Use simple present tense to describe your work. Use simple past tense to describe already published work.

Define EVERY acronym (e.g., TSP) when it first appears (e.g., traveling salesman problem (TSP)). Don't define any acronyms that you don't intend to re-use later in the report. Define EVERY math symbol when it first appears in the report. Avoid inventing new phrases, new terminologies, or new acronyms unless it is absolutely essential.

Use standard forms of references, for example (must include author names, paper title, journal/conference title, page/volume number for journal, year, etc. Note there should a space at appropriate places.),
[1]     J. C. Maxwell, A Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism, 3rd ed., vol. 2. Oxford: Clarendon, 1892, pp.68–73.

[2]     Y. Yorozu, M. Hirano, K. Oka, and Y. Tagawa, “Electron spectroscopy studies on magneto-optical media and plastic substrate interface,” IEEE Trans. Industrial Electronics, vol. 2, pp. 740–741, August 1987.

Each reference must have publication title and year. For a journal reference, make sure it also has journal name, volume number, and page number. For a conference reference, make sure it has conference name. For a book reference, make sure it has publisher name and publisher city. There should be at least 40 references in your PROJECT.
In the literature survey part, leave out things that are too elementary, for example, you don’t need a figure showing the old 3-layer multilayer perceptron neural network.

When citing someone, use their surnames only. Don't include first names or initials. For example, say "Chua [5] proposed..." (suppose the paper cited is reference #5), not "L.O. Chua proposed...". When citing a paper with two authors, include both authors' names, not only one of the authors. When citing a paper with 3 or more authors, use either et al or include all authors names, for example, Lee et al... or Lee, Lin, and Wang.... Don’t use “The research paper …” or “The comparison paper …”.

Write simple and short sentences, unless you are absolutely sure that the long sentences you write are clear and correct. Make sure each sentence uses correct grammar. DO NOT use abbreviations like "don't", "can't".
Number all equations, figures, tables, etc, so that they can be referred to easily.
For each figure/plot/table:

1.       If the width of the figure is about 6cm (about half of A4 page width), the font size of labels (words/numbers) for the axis or inside the figure must be 8 or 9, so that it is big enough to read. The size of the axis label should be increased proportionally, so that when the figure is reduced to 6cm-wide later, the axis label is still big enough to read.
2.       Minimize the number of words inside of a figure. Explain the figure in the figure legend.

3.       Do not use color in figures. Instead, use different line types (dashes, solid), different dots, squares, triangles, etc. Do not have too many of these symbols in figures to make it hard to tell which is which.
4.       Avoid grids inside a figure
5.       Do not have too many ticks on each axis (for example, no more than 6 ticks for each axis).
6.       Each figure or table must have a legend, a concise description of the figure/table. Do not use shades or colors in tables.
7.       Make sure all figures have high resolution. If you need to capture screen, enlarge the figure first and then capture the screen.
8.       Avoid figure titles (labels on top of the figures). Have description in figure legends instead.
9.       All plotted figures should have axis and all axis must have labels (i.e., explain what is plotted against what).

No need to include codes in your report. If you want to include codes, put them in an Appendix, not in the main chapters. Describe your algorithms in English (or pseudocodes) and/or block diagrams/figures.
Whenever possible/appropriate, compare your results with published results based on the same dataset by listing both results in the same table or plotting both results in the same figure.
Include the sources of datasets used in your references.
Email me both Word (or Latex) file and PDF file of your PROJECT report. I myself do not need any hardcopies (I don’t speak for any other examiners).

When you submit your final version (after your updates according to comments from me and the examiner), also submit your source codes and data files necessary to run the codes, plus a brief instruction on how to run your codes. These things are not needed for the examiner. Only for me. If it is too big to email, upload somewhere (e.g., dropsend.com) and give me a download link.
Submissions

After you email me your thesis, I usually need a few days to read it and may give you some suggestions to improve/revise. Then you may need to spend time revising and send me again. If you don’t revise adequately, the process may repeat. After you submit to school, the review will take time. Please don’t email me your thesis and expect me to sign it immediately. I heard that you can still submit thesis after STP expires (but you need to verify this). If you need to graduate or take a job at a certain date, you should send thesis to me at least 2-3 months before that date.
When your thesis is ready for final submission to school, please also send the following to me (not to school):
Program source codes (with a readme file briefly explaining which file is for what purpose. See “Project-Code and Reproducibility Requirements” below for details).
Thesis Word (or Latex) file.

All figures that you draw in editable forms. For example, if you draw a figure using PPT, send me the ppt file. If you draw in Word, that’s fine to send me the Word file. Diagrams in screen shots (likely copied from somewhere) are not acceptable.
Regular Backup

It is very important to back up all your data frequently (as frequent as you care to loss the data, since your disk might become corrupted at any time). If a student says no submissions can be made because of computer failure, this will not be considered a valid excuse.
Initial (Introductory) Meeting?
I don’t require this. If you need one, please let me know what we will be discussing. Otherwise, we can have a discussion when you have some results to discuss.
Things that I am not able to help
·         Debug a program
·         Solve computer issues
Set up a detailed timeline and milestones
·         Teach how neural networks work
Major Mistakes
·         Ignored my instructions given in this email (they said they read this email, but they didn’t really read it)
Never email progress to me, do all the wrong things, and suddenly tell me I must sign their thesis NOW!
Project-Code and Reproducibility Requirements
The aim of these requirements is not to create production-quality software.The aim is simply that, at the end of the project:
The supervisor can run the code without guessing missing files.
The main experimental results in the dissertation can be approximately reproduced.
Another student can continue the work if necessary.
The expectations are lightweight and focus on good organization rather than heavy documentation.
1. Folder Structure (Keep It Simple)
Use a clear top-level project folder such as:
project_name/
code/
configs/
data_readme.txt
results/
logs/
thesis_tables/
You do not need complicated subfolders.The important part is consistency.
2. Version Control (Minimum Requirement)
Use Git (GitHub, GitLab, or private repository).
Minimum rules:
Commit at least once per week.
Each commit message can be short, e.g.,“add PQW weighting module”“VOC split2 experiments”
No need for branching strategies or advanced workflows.
This alone prevents most “lost code” problems.
3. One Main Entry Script
At the end of the project there must be:
One training script
One evaluation script
Example names:
train.py
test.py
They do not need to be elegant.They just need to run.
4. Configuration Files Instead of Hard-Coding
Store hyperparameters in a small config file rather than editing code every time.
Example:
configs/voc_split1_5shot.yaml
Even a simple .txt or .json file is fine.
This avoids the “which parameters did I use?” problem.
5. Record Final Experiment Settings
For every table or figure in the thesis:
Create one small text file in thesis_tables/ such as:
table5_2_settings.txt
Content example (5–10 lines only):
Dataset: VOC Split1
Shot: 5
Seed: 42
Epochs: 12
Checkpoint: model_voc_s1_5shot_seed42.pth
No long explanations needed.Just enough to rerun the experiment.
6. Logs and Checkpoints
Keep at least one final checkpoint per main experiment.
Keep one log file showing the final metrics.
Old intermediate logs can be deleted if disk space is limited.
7. Data Handling
You do not need to redistribute datasets.
Instead, include a small file:
data_readme.txt
Example:
Dataset: PASCAL VOC 2007+2012
Download from: official website
Expected path: /data/voc/
8. Minimal Documentation (Maximum 1–2 Pages)
At the end, provide one README file with:
Environment (Python version, major libraries)
How to train
How to test
Approximate runtime
GPU/CPU requirement
This should be 1–2 pages maximum.No detailed API documentation required.
9. Reproducibility Expectation Level
The requirement is approximate reproducibility, not exact bit-wise matching.
Acceptable:
±1–2% metric difference
Slight training variance
Not acceptable:
Code cannot run
Missing modules
Unknown parameters
10. End-of-Project Submission Checklist
At submission time, the student should provide:
Full source code folder
Config files
Final checkpoints
Logs for main experiments
README (1–2 pages)
Thesis tables’ setting files
No extra polishing required.
Guiding Principle
“Code should be runnable and understandable, not perfect.”
The goal is continuity and verification, not software engineering excellence.Following these simple habits adds only small overhead during the project but prevents major problems at the end.
# 项目全文中文翻译
**标题：基于视觉语言模型实现机器人操作策略零样本泛化的机器学习研究**

让机器人在非结构化环境中操控物理物体，是具身人工智能领域的核心难题之一。传统机器人学习方法需要在目标环境下采集大量面向特定任务的演示数据，很难拓展到全新任务与场景。大型视觉语言模型的最新进展，为利用模型内部蕴含的丰富语义知识引导机器人策略，处理训练阶段从未见过的物体与任务指令提供了可能性。本课题研究如何对预训练视觉语言模型做适配改造，将其作为桌面机器人操作的零样本策略模块；依托仿真环境与公开演示数据集，实现机械臂理解自然语言指令、交互未见过物体的能力。本课题不要求学生预先掌握机器人学或机器学习知识，课题会向参与学生提供详细指导文档与数据集。
**创新点**
现有视觉语言驱动的机器人操作方案存在两类局限：一类需要使用成千上万条机器人演示样本对大模型做全量微调，成本高昂；另一类仅依靠大语言模型完成高层任务拆解，底层控制交由单独训练的基础技能实现。
本课题提出轻量化适配器架构：在冻结的视觉语言模型主干网络与基于扩散模型的动作解码器之间接入少量可训练的交叉注意力层。仅对适配器参数使用少量演示样本微调，大预训练模型本身保持冻结。
核心创新为**反事实数据增强策略**：训练时固定视觉场景，系统性改写语言指令；或是固定语言指令、改动视觉场景。迫使适配器把视觉特征与语言语义解耦，最终让策略在测试阶段面对指令转述、物体外观变化时鲁棒性大幅提升。
这种参数高效适配结合反事实指令增强的方案尚未出现在现有机器人学习文献中，解决了通用机器人策略落地部署的关键瓶颈。

**研究问题**
1. 核心研究问题：基于Open XEmbodiment数据集的少量样本训练得到轻量化交叉注意力适配器，在LIBERO、CLIPort基准测试集的全新物体、全新指令任务上，零样本任务成功率能否达到甚至超过全量微调的基线模型。
2. 次要问题：相比传统数据增强，反事实指令增强策略能否显著提升模型面对指令转述的鲁棒性；评估方式为同一物理任务，使用语义等价但措辞不同的多条指令做测试。
3. 第三个研究问题：适配器是否具备跨机器人硬件泛化能力；即使用Open XEmbodiment中某一类机械臂样本训练，测试时控制另一款仿真机械臂，性能是否可以维持在可用水平。
**详细研究方案与方法**
本项目分为四个阶段：
1. **第一阶段（约3个月）**：搭建ManiSkill2或PyBullet仿真环境，下载全部4个公开数据集；编写统一数据加载器，把不同来源演示样本解析为统一格式：自然语言指令字符串、224×224像素RGB图像序列、8维末端执行器动作序列（位置+四元数+夹爪开度）。过滤样本，仅保留带有效语言标注、动作序列至少10个时间步的演示数据。

2. **第二阶段（约5个月）**：实现适配器架构。主干网络采用冻结的CLIP ViTL/14视觉语言模型，视觉、文本编码器输出1024维嵌入特征。适配器包含8层交叉注意力层（Key/Value维度512），部署在CLIP编码器之后；输入视觉Token序列与语言嵌入，输出融合上下文向量。融合向量送入基于DDPM、UNet降噪网络的条件扩散动作解码器；输入为带噪声的动作轨迹与融合上下文，输出降噪后的动作轨迹。训练仅更新适配器与扩散解码器，CLIP全部权重冻结。
3. **第三阶段（约4个月）**：实现反事实增强策略。
- 针对每一条训练样本，生成反事实样本：保持原始场景，替换为同一任务集下目标不同的其他指令，动作序列置全零，教会模型：场景指令不匹配时应当输出无动作。
- 转述增强：本地部署大模型，为每条原始指令生成5条措辞不同但语义一致的复述，作为额外正样本。
- 设置四组对照训练：无增强、仅转述增强、仅反事实增强、完整组合增强。
- 仿真环境评估：每个任务划分下运行100轮仿真，**任务成功率作为核心评价指标**。
4. **第四阶段（约2个月）**：消融实验，逐层移除适配器层，确定保证性能所需的最小层数；跨硬件迁移实验：在Open XEmbodiment某一类机器人样本训练，仿真环境另一类机器人上测试。定性分析：固定单一模态、改变另一模态，区分模型失败来自视觉歧义还是语言歧义。

Thank you for the careful analysis. These are good questions and your thinking is already heading in the right direction.

On the Bridge Dataset, the BridgeData V2 version included in the Open X-Embodiment repository under the dataset name "bridge" is indeed the same underlying dataset collected on the WidowX robot, with 25,460 episodes. This is the version you should use, and it is the one cited as Walke et al. (CoRL 2023) in the project. The original URL at rail.eecs.berkeley.edu appears to have gone offline, but since the Open X-Embodiment copy is already in a unified RLDS format that your data loader will be reading anyway, using it from there is the correct and convenient choice. On the Open X-Embodiment filtering strategy, your proposed criteria are sensible as a starting point, but I want to be more precise about what the thesis must do, because the filtering decisions themselves need to be treated as a documented experimental choice rather than just a preprocessing step. The thesis must clearly state and justify the inclusion and exclusion criteria applied to the Open X-Embodiment subsets, and the cross-embodiment transfer experiment must still be designed around this. Here is what I recommend. For the main adapter training and evaluation experiments, restrict to subsets that satisfy all three of your proposed conditions: single-arm manipulator, EEF position control, and natural language annotations. Applying this filter to the dataset overview, the subsets that qualify and have a meaningful number of episodes include fractal20220817_data (RT-1, 73,499 episodes, templated language), bridge (25,460 episodes, natural language), language_table (442,226 episodes, natural language), bc_z (39,350 episodes, templated language), viola (135 episodes, templated language), berkeley_autolab_ur5 (896 episodes, templated language), austin_mutex (1,500 episodes, natural language), berkeley_fanuc_manipulation (415 episodes, natural language), and utaustin_mutex is already listed. Since your adapter's cross-attention alignment between language and visual features is the key technical claim, you should report results separately for natural-language-annotated subsets versus templated-language subsets, as the paraphrase robustness evaluation is most meaningful for the former. This breakdown must appear as a table in the thesis. Note also that the language_table subset uses a stick-pushing end effector rather than a standard gripper, so you should document whether you include or exclude it and why; if you include it, note the action space difference.

For the cross-embodiment transfer experiment, which is one of the research questions in the project plan, you need to deliberately train on demonstrations from one robot type and evaluate on another. A natural pair given the filtered subsets is to train on the WidowX data from bridge and evaluate on a simulated version of the Franka robot using ManiSkill2 or PyBullet, since the Franka appears in many subsets (viola, austin_mutex, stanford_hydra, and others) and is readily available in simulation.
